walkthroughs.body_html:
Animal Physiology — a core area of Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Animal Physiology brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Animal Physiology.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Burnet's clonal selection theory of immunity dates from:

options: Inserting aquaporins in collecting duct
Closing aquaporins
Increasing glomerular filtration
Stimulating renin

mcqs.q: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker muscular wall than the right?
options: The left ventricle is thicker because it is on the same side as the brain.
It must pump blood at high pressure around the whole body; the right ventricle only pumps to the nearby lungs.
Prokaryotes are always smaller than 1 micrometre and have no cytoplasm.
The left ventricle is thicker because it handles oxygenated blood, which is harder to pump.

mcqs.q: What is the role of the guide RNA in CRISPR-Cas9?
options: Guide RNA is the enzyme that cuts the DNA.
It directs Cas9 to the specific DNA sequence to cut by base-pairing with the target.
Prokaryotes are always smaller than 1 micrometre and have no cytoplasm.
Guide RNA is the new sequence that gets inserted into the genome.

mcqs.q: What is the key structural difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
options: Eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotes do not.
Prokaryotes have no DNA — that's why they have no nucleus.
The left ventricle is thicker because it is on the same side as the brain.
Prokaryotes are always smaller than 1 micrometre and have no cytoplasm.
